rationale_project: The Basin’s Sahelian zone is an endemic zone covering migratory locust (Schistocerca gregaria) outbreak areas. It is regularly invaded by crop-devouring pests (locusts, grasshoppers, insect borers, hairy caterpillars, cantharides, seed-eating birds, rodents, diseases and weeds), causing a substantial drop in yields. Such pests can cause losses of up to 50% of production. Striga hermonthica for instance is capable of damaging over 60% of production.
GESI_project: Women represented 24% of pilot farmers (29 women out of 120) trained in Farmer Field Schools. Their participation in the FFS activities was highly satisfactory, averaging above 70%. Concerning mentorship, at least 20% of extension workers trained were women. The presence of women extension workers facilitated the active participation of rural pilot women farmers. This training afforded them the opportunity to benefit from innovations, enhance their capacity to upgrade their production techniques and respond to market opportunities. It also enabled farmers to substantially increase their food production and income, improve their health and that of their families, manage their resources and strengthen their participation in decision-making. Those who own individual fields experimented integrated pest management techniques in their fields, and taught such techniques to other women who were not members of their village brigades and even those from nearby villages. This means that the application of integrated pest management by women farmers is of very special importance. Hence, this population segment should be advised against using harmful and persistent products in pest control. The impact on gender is not satisfactory, considering the low representation of women in the structures put in place, including the pilot farmers, and non-removal of barriers to women's access to factors of production. The project's impact on gender is unsatisfactory.

rationale_project: To address pastoralists’ vulnerabilities arising from more frequent and severe crises (drought, food insecurity and conflict), growing restrictions on mobility and access to natural resources (due to changing land use, development schemes and border controls), trans-boundary animal diseases, and risks from climate change, insecurity and economic shocks, by delivering regional public goods—animal disease control, sustainable rangeland and water management, market facilitation, and crisis preparedness—to improve productivity, sustainability and resilience of pastoral livelihoods.
GESI_project: The project recognized that women are socio-economic agents in their own right and are indispensable to the survival of pastoral communities. In this regard, it was the aim of the project in particular to strengthen pastoral women’s capacity to support external shocks including those related to conflicts. PRAPS was therefore designed to systematically mainstream women’s specific concerns and needs pertinent to women into its activities, and address the most salient gender gaps. All activities undertaken throughout the project had to demonstrate that gender issues were addressed whenever possible. The Regional Project Coordination Unit (R-PCU) and the National Project Coordination Unites (N-PCUs) recruited gender focal points fluent in the local language to ensure that women participated actively during consultations and were duly represented in all major decision-making entities. Gender action plans were implemented at national level, and a regional gender assessment was conducted as part of the Mid-Term Review. All data collected on project beneficiaries were systematically gender disaggregated by the M&E units, as well as data on specific project activities such as IGAs. These data revealed that the target set for the percentage of women beneficiaries had been exceeded (33 percent vs. 30 percent target), and, in the case of the small IGA program, was surpassed by a large margin (86 percent vs. the 50 percent target).

project_title: Burundi - Coffee Sector Competitiveness Project
project_lead: NEW: Ministry of Environment, Agriculture and Livestock
rationale_project: The project was to address the key constraints of Burundi’s coffee value chain: governance inefficiencies due to incomplete liberalization and privatization; low productivity and declining production levels due to insufficient technical and financial support, poor maintenance and degradation of orchards, low input use, and pests and diseases; limited competitiveness from aging orchards and weak producer capacity; imbalance between primary production and processing; weak transport infrastructure and landlocked export costs; and sensitive political economy related to agricultural production and land tenure.
GESI_project: Sub-Component 1.4: Women and youth empowerment (US$0.68 million), in recognition of the large gender gap in Burundi, included the preparation of a stand-alone comprehensive coffee gender and youth strategy and a matching grant program to promote women and youth entrepreneurial activities through sub-projects designed to support coffee productive activities, particularly those promoting land and resource preservation, climate-smart infrastructure and energy saving. Given the significant gender gap in the coffee value chain, the project was gender-tagged. Its objective was to reach 30 percent of women as part of its direct beneficiaries. Activities specifically designed to address the specific needs of vulnerable groups, including women in terms of coffee productivity with a focus on environmental concerns, were implemented through a small matching grants program under Sub-Component 1.4. Twenty - eight sub-projects totaling US$423,000 were funded and benefitted 776 people of whom 573 were women. To deliver on its gender program, the project recruited a gender specialist in 2018 and commissioned a Gender Strategy for the coffee value chain. However, no action plan was prepared under the strategy, and no specialized data was collected. project_title: PPCR Evaluation Report
location_notes: Document reports a total of 18 pilot countries and two regions (Caribbean and Paciﬁc); of the pilot and additional pilot countries listed, 9 are in Africa (Mozambique, Niger, Zambia, Ethiopia, the Gambia, Madagascar, Malawi, Rwanda, Uganda).
rationale_project: The PPCR’s stated goal is to integrate climate resilience into countries’ core development planning and provide incentives for scaled up action and transformational change and to pilot and demonstrate ways to build resilience that could guide future adaptation initiatives.
GESI_project: PPCR programming expanded its gender focus since its inception, but sustainability remains a challenge. Most SPCRs and PPCR projects were approved before the CIF introduced Gender Action Plans in 2014 and 2016 and a Gender Policy in 2018. Moreover, most SPCRs gave minimal attention to integrating gender equality into adaptation approaches and investments. Most project designs identiﬁed women as beneﬁciaries but about three-quarters lacked details on addressing vulnerabilities or promoting inclusivity. Projects targeting youth (47%), the elderly (22%), Indigenous Peoples or racial minorities (21%), and disabled people (9%) were even fewer. Despite the limited reporting on disadvantaged groups, women have accounted for about half of PPCR beneﬁciaries, and some projects achieved notable results, such as reduced time burdens among women and girls for water collection, a reduced gender gap in agricultural productivity, and enhanced economic empowerment through livelihood support, job creation, and access to ﬁnancing and services. Some projects also increased their focus on gender during implementation. In Tajikistan, a project to increase access to loans added gender targets, gender sensitivity training, and incentives for institutions serving women in its second phase. As a result, the project’s female sub-borrowers reported social, economic, and climate resilience beneﬁts alongside empowerment co-beneﬁts. That said, equity issues persisted after projects closed in some cases. In Mozambique, only wealthier farmer associations could continue to afford the fuel costs previously covered by the project. In Bangladesh, reserved market stalls for female traders disappeared within four years of the project’s completion.
